title: Design Smells and Common Anti-Patterns
learningObjectives: Recognize common design smells without treating them as automatic defects.
Explain why long functions and excessive coupling can be warning signs.
Identify duplicated logic, hidden state, and unclear boundaries.
Choose a proportionate improvement for a design smell.
Avoid blindly applying patterns or rules without context.

understand.concept: A design smell is a signal that code may be harder to understand, change, or test than necessary. Examples include very long functions, duplicated logic, too many responsibilities, hidden global state, excessive parameters, and components that know too much about each other. A smell is not proof of a bug: context matters, and the simplest effective improvement may be enough. Anti-patterns are recurring approaches that tend to create avoidable problems, such as using shared mutable state as an informal communication channel.
understand.whyItMatters: Clear design boundaries and intentional development practices help teams maintain software, verify changes, and respond to real needs.
understand.analogy: Think of a team coordinating a shared task: clear responsibilities and feedback loops help everyone work toward the same result.
understand.analogyLimit: Software design includes precise technical constraints and interactions that teamwork analogies cannot fully represent.

explain.narrative: When you notice a smell, first understand what the code does and why it exists. Look for the cost it creates—confusing changes, repeated fixes, test difficulty, or side effects. Then make a small improvement and verify behavior. Do not refactor merely to make code look like a textbook pattern; unnecessary rewrites can introduce risk.

examples.title: Spot a long mixed-purpose function
examples.explanation: The function performs several steps that may have separate responsibilities.

examples.title: Avoid duplicate calculation
examples.explanation: A helper avoids repeated expression logic when it represents the same concept.

examples.title: Recognize hidden state
examples.explanation: A global variable makes behavior depend on shared state.

examples.title: Reduce unnecessary parameters
examples.explanation: A focused function needs only the data it uses.

examples.title: Choose a small improvement
examples.explanation: A focused helper is clearer than embedding the same rule in many places.

commonMistakes: Treating design smells as automatic defects.
Overengineering small projects with unnecessary layers or patterns.
Mixing requirements, features, and refactoring without clear intent.
Ignoring tests or edge cases when changing structure.
Failing to consider project context and trade-offs.

guidedTask.title: Guided Practice
guidedTask.instructions: Review a sample and list possible smells without changing it. Choose the one smell that most affects clarity or change. Propose a small fix rather than a full rewrite. Apply the fix and compare the behavior. Explain why the smell was a warning, not an automatic verdict.

independentTask.title: Independent Practice
independentTask.instructions: Create or select a small program containing two design smells. Describe the maintenance cost of each smell. Fix one smell with a small change. Add a test or trace to show behavior is preserved. Explain why you did not rewrite everything.
requirements: Create or select a small program containing two design smells.
Describe the maintenance cost of each smell.
Fix one smell with a small change.
Add a test or trace to show behavior is preserved.
Explain why you did not rewrite everything.
